 Tens of thousands of Mainers could lose both food and health care under Trump’s “Big Beautiful Bill”
 James Myall 
 November 3, 2026 
 Categories: 
 Health Care , Maine’s Economy 
 Tags: 
 Federal , Food Insecurity , Health Care , Medicaid , SNAP 
 At a glance:
 In January, new work rules could cause about 27,000 Mainers to lose both MaineCare health coverage and SNAP food assistance
 Adults under age 64 without kids under 14 must work or volunteer 80 hours a month or earn at least $580
 Many people lose benefits by mistake because of confusion or paperwork errors —23,000 Mainers, including 7,000 kids, have already lost SNAP
 Lawmakers can cut paperwork, fund outreach, and give people extra time to finish forms
 New analysis from MECEP finds when MaineCare work reporting requirements take effect in January, about 27,000 Mainers could lose both health coverage and Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits.
 The so-called “One Big Beautiful Bill” (OBBB) passed by Congress in July last year expanded SNAP work reporting requirements and added them to Medicaid (called MaineCare in Maine) for the first time. As a result, tens of thousands of Mainers could lose both kinds of assistance at a time when Mainers are feeling especially squeezed by high prices.
 The new requirements apply to adults under age 64 1 who don’t have children younger than 14. There are also exemptions for people who can prove they have a disability, are getting treatment for substance use disorder, or who suffer from other medical conditions. Exactly which conditions qualify for an exemption and how people can prove it is still unclear and is the subject of an ongoing lawsuit. Mainers who don’t qualify for an exemption will have to show they engaged in 80 hours of work or volunteer activities per month or earned at least $580.
 However, the number of Mainers who could lose public assistance is likely to be much higher than those who don’t meet these requirements. Evidence from prior work requirement programs shows large numbers of people don’t understand the changes and drop off the program because they think they aren’t eligible or they file paperwork incorrectly and lose benefits when they shouldn’t. Maine is seeing this in SNAP, where have lost benefits since the passage of OBBB. The losses among children, whose eligibility did not change, illustrates the collateral damage from OBBB.
 According to MECEP’s analysis of Census Bureau and Maine DHHS data, the following groups will be subject to the work requirements: 2 
 Around 27,000 Mainers receiving both SNAP and MaineCare
 Another 45,000 Mainers enrolled in MaineCare but without SNAP
 Another 19,000 Mainers enrolled in SNAP but not MaineCare
 These numbers do not include children, of whom there are more than 100,000 in the MaineCare program alone. If even a small share loses MaineCare coverage due to misunderstandings of the new rules, thousands of kids could end up uninsured.
 Prior MECEP research has shown Mainers most at risk from these cuts are in the more rural parts of the state, where work is harder to find and lower household incomes mean more people rely on SNAP and MaineCare to make ends meet.
 State lawmakers need to do everything they can to help Mainers keep access to these crucial assistance programs. This can include ensuring the state uses data effectively, investing in community partnerships to reach out to vulnerable Mainers (which states like New York are already doing), and using state funds to provide a “bridge period” for Mainers who are at risk of losing coverage and need more time to complete their paperwork.
 Congress also has the power to avert economic harm for tens of thousands of Mainers and millions nationwide, either when it comes back in December for its “lame duck” session, or with the inauguration of a new Congress in 2027. For the benefit of Americans with low income nationwide, lawmakers should roll back these destructive and burdensome work requirements as much as possible. 
 Notes:
 [1] The work reporting requirements begin at age 18 for SNAP and age 19 for Medicaid.
 [2] MECEP analysis of US Census Bureau, American Community Survey data, 2020-2024 average, and Maine DHHS data on Medicaid expansion enrollment for childless adults as of August 2026. MECEP used ACS data for the share of 19- to 64-year-olds without children age 14 or over who were not enrolled in Social Security or Medicare to determine the population subject to the work requirements. In the ACS data, 37% of Medicaid enrollees with these characteristics were also in households that received SNAP benefits. This percentage was applied to the 72,592 childless adults enrolled in MaineCare as of August 2026 per Maine DHHS.
 James Myall 
 James is MECEP’s lead on the inclusive economy, including research on labor issues, gender and racial equity, and health care policy. 
James conducts research and impact analyses, writes educational materials, and collaborates with partners. He is skilled in data collection, research, and statistical and policy analysis. He studied public policy and management at the University of Southern Maine and holds a master’s degree in ancient history and archaeology from the University of St. Andrews in Scotland.
